title: Olympic Beach Volleyball: Road to Gold
text:
Atlanta 1996 — Paris 2024



Follow beach volleyball from its Olympic debut to a new generation of champions. This story uses athlete-event records to put the sport in the wider Olympic picture—and team results to trace every medal.

Explore the data →

title: Olympic Beach Volleyball: Road to Gold
text:
One Olympic timeline, three lenses
The broadest view follows every Summer Olympic athlete-event entry. The gold trace then zooms in: first on all indoor and beach Volleyball entries, then on beach volleyball alone, identified from the event field. Each panel has its own vertical scale so the specialist event remains visible.





Athlete-event entries at Summer Olympic Games. Panels use separate vertical scales.










NoteWhat counts as a record?



One row represents one athlete at one Games edition in one event—not one unique person or one team. The source has 315,094 rows; the chart aggregates the 250,747 Summer Games rows. Beach volleyball is filtered from event within the Volleyball sport, rather than treating all Volleyball entries as beach volleyball.


Sources: olympicAthletes package and data documentation. See methodology and results sources for team-medal counting and the recent podium supplement.

What those medals are made of
The next chart compares gold, silver, and bronze team medals by country. Hover for exact counts. Country totals include both men’s and women’s events across 1996–2024.






Data note: the 2020 and 2024 athlete-event records do not carry beach-volleyball medal labels in this release of the source. Their podium teams are added from the Tokyo 2020 results and Paris 2024 results, not inferred from missing values.

title: Road to Gold
text:
Since beach volleyball joined the Olympic programme in 1996, Brazil has earned 14 team medals, including 4 golds. Brazil reached the podium at every Games from 1996 through 2016, then returned to the top of the women’s podium in Paris. The United States is next with 11 medals, 7 of them gold, built across both men’s and women’s events.
Success has never belonged to just two flags. Australia won women’s gold in 2000; Germany’s golds came in the men’s event in 2012 and the women’s in 2016; and China took silver and bronze in the 2008 women’s competition. More recently, Norway and Sweden captured men’s gold in Tokyo and Paris, while Qatar earned men’s bronze at both editions.

title: Road to Gold
text:
Every medal, counted once
The chart counts a medal for the country-team pair in an event, not for each athlete on that pair. Each edition awards three medals in each of two events, giving 48 team medals across eight editions.





Beach volleyball team medals by country and medal type, 1996–2024.

title: Road to Gold
text:
Methodology

The source is olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes, a 315,094-row, 16-column athlete-event dataset. The package describes 1896–2016 records as extending the Olympic history dataset, with later records sourced from Olympedia.
Beach volleyball is selected by requiring sport == "Volleyball" and a beach-volleyball match in event. The package’s 4,792-row volleyball_athletes subset contains indoor and beach volleyball; it is not used as a beach-volleyball count.
For 1996–2016, the source repeats the medal on both athletes’ rows. We retain one row for each Games year, event, team identifier, and medal, then normalize team suffixes (such as -1) only when aggregating results by country.
The package data used here has no beach-volleyball medal labels for 2020 or 2024. We add the six podium teams for each of those editions from the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 official results pages. These are team-level rows, so no athlete-level medal duplication is introduced.
Participation charts count athlete-event rows; medal charts count medal-winning teams. A pair therefore contributes two participation records but only one medal.
To render the site, install R packages olympicAthletes, tidyverse, ggplot2, plotly, and crosstalk, then run quarto render.

For other country results, edition details, and filters, head to Explore the Olympics.
